### Firearm injury health encounters and county-level poverty

3.3
Adjusting for age, race, sex, and urbanicity, individuals living in counties in the highest poverty tertile had 3.6 times higher (95% CI: 2.7–4.8) total firearm injury health encounters compared to those living in counties in the lowest poverty tertile and this difference was statistically significant (Fig. 1). Those living in counties in the intermediate poverty tertile had an adjusted 1.2 times higher (95% CI: 0.9–1.6) total firearm injury health encounters compared to those living in the lowest county poverty tertile, but this difference was not statistically significant.

We observed statistically significant increases in the adjusted firearm injury health encounters incidence rate ratios in counties in the highest poverty tertile category for firearm-related assaults (IRR: 5.5, 95% CI: 3.8–8.0), and unintentional (IRR: 3.2, 95% CI: 2.1–4.6),However, there was no statistically significant difference in the adjusted firearm self-harm incidence rate when comparing individuals residing in counties in the highest poverty tertile (IRR: 1.9, 95% CI: 1.0–3.7) to those residing in the lowest poverty tertile.

## Discussion

4
In this ecological study, counties in the highest poverty tertile had higher rates of overall firearm injury health encounters including assault, self-harm, and unintentional intent compared to counties in the lowest poverty tertile. This association was present, for most injury intents, after adjusting for other relevant factors such as age, race, sex, and urbanicity, that are known to contribute to the occurrence of firearm injuries [11,12,24]. This study is consistent with similar studies conducted on the national level demonstrating higher rates of firearm injuries in counties with higher poverty concentration. To our knowledge, this is the first study evaluating county poverty concentration and firearm injury health encounters across various intents in the State of Maryland.

The United States has one of the highest poverty rates among developed countries with the greatest burden among racial minority communities [17]. Poverty is a multifaceted construct that goes beyond income and includes economic well-being, social exclusion, lack of basic education and employment opportunities, and inadequate housing [17,25]. It is recognized as one of the most significant factors contributing to poor health outcomes [26]. Prior studies have linked poverty to violence and subsequent injuries, mental health conditions, and communicable and non-communicable diseases [11,12,17]. This impact of poverty is consistent with our study findings that show that individuals residing in counties with the highest poverty concentration comprise 52% of firearm injury health encounters in the state though they make up only 16% of the total population.

The link between poverty and firearm violence intersects with other deeply entrenched socioeconomic factors like racism [17]. Persistent systemic and structural racism in the United States contribute to the higher burden of firearm violence in racial minority communities [18]. In this study, we observed higher rates of overall health encounter firearm injuries and firearm-related assault and unintentional injuries in Black individuals compared to their White counterparts. Systemic racism plays a role in these findings through concentrated poverty, socioeconomic deprivation, and increased surveillance and harassment by law enforcement in minority communities [18]. While we did not identify which firearm injury health encounters occurred due to police encounters in our analysis; there is strong evidence linking policing and firearm violence among racial minorities [18,27,28]. In contrast to the pattern of increased firearm-related assaults among Black individuals, we found higher rates of firearm-related self-harm in White individuals, which is consistent with prior literature [12,29]. American Indian/Alaska Native populations are second to White populations in rates of firearm-related suicides nationally [12,29], but the population characteristics in the State of Maryland did now allow for this analysis.

We observed significantly higher firearm injury health encounter rates in counties in the highest poverty tertile compared to those in the lowest poverty tertile, but we did not observe significant increases when comparing counties in the intermediate poverty tertile to those in the lowest poverty tertile. This suggests the impact of poverty may be more pronounced at higher poverty levels. The significantly higher firearm injury health encounter rates seen in counties in the highest poverty tertile was consistent across overall firearm injuries and intents, except for firearm-related self-harm injuries which did not show significant differences in firearm injury rates across poverty tertiles. This suggests that there are other factors that contribute to the association between county-level poverty and firearm-related self-harm such as firearm prevalence and access to mental health services [12,30] that were not accounted for in this study due to limited data.

The highest rates of overall health encounter firearm injuries and firearm-related assaults and unintentional injuries were observed among those aged 15–24. This is consistent with data from the literature demonstrating sharp increases in firearm-related injuries in US youth, particularly in the 15-24 year-old age group, with homicides increasing by 14% over the past decade [2]. Increased access to firearms has been cited as one of the main causes of this phenomenon [2]. Federal law restricts licensed dealers from selling or transferring handguns and long guns to minors, and Maryland law generally prohibits anyone under age 21 from possessing a handgun or other regulated firearm as well as prohibiting any person from selling or transferring a firearm or ammunition to a person under age 18 [2,[[31]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12886088/#bib31), [[32]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12886088/#bib32), [[33]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12886088/#bib33), [[34]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12886088/#bib34)]. In addition, the presence of firearms in the home is a significant risk factor in firearm-related injuries among youth [35] with estimates of firearm ownership in Maryland between 16 and 20% [36,37]. While studies show firearm-related self-harm has also been increasing among the 15–24 age group [38,39], we observed the highest rates of firearm-related self-harm among the 35–44 age group followed by similar rates in the 15–24 age group and ≥45 age group. This effect may be due to known increases in firearm self-harm rates with age [40] and firearms being the most common method of self-harm in older adults [41].

Differences in firearm injury rates are known to exist between rural and urban counties [11,12,42]. In this study, we observed higher overall firearm injury health encounter rates and firearm-related assaults in urban counties compared to rural counties. In contrast, we found higher rates of unintentional and self-harm firearm injury health encounters in rural counties compared to urban counties, consistent with previous studies [12,42]. This finding highlights the probability of other mechanisms that influence the association between urbanicity and firearm injuries by self-harm and unintentional intent compared to other intents. This includes higher lethality of means of suicide and increased accessibility to firearms in rural counties [12,24]. In Maryland specifically, victims of firearm suicide in rural counties were more likely to use long guns compared to most urban counties even after adjusting for demographic factors and hunting season [24]. While data on firearm ownership by county in Maryland is limited, one of the top reasons for gun ownership in the United States is hunting, and rural areas are known to engage more in hunting activities [43].

Our study findings indicate that county-level poverty is associated with the occurrence of firearm injury health encounters in Maryland. We emphasize that reducing firearm injuries in Maryland, a state with a higher firearm homicide rate compared to the national rate, requires a multisector approach including legislation on restricting firearm access, addressing attitudes towards gun violence, and tackling social determinants of health like poverty from the individual to the societal level. The association between poverty and firearm injuries intersects with other socioeconomic factors beyond income status including inadequate housing and a limited number of and access to resources [17,25]. These factors contribute to a breakdown in social cohesion described as a lack of mutual trust among community members that contributes to firearm violence [44]. Sustainable reduction of firearm injuries therefore requires consideration of these factors in the creation and implementation of policies. The Baltimore Safe Streets Intervention is an example of an existing community-based program that has shown significant results in improving youth attitudes towards gun violence, a known factor contributing to gun violence in high-risk youth [45]. Community efforts such as these that address sociocultural factors that underlie poverty, policies that target job, food, and housing insecurities, and higher-level societal interventions on restricting gun access and promoting safe gun storage are necessary to address the complexity of the factors contributing to firearm violence [46,47].

### Study limitations and strengths

4.1
This study has several limitations. First, because this is an ecological study, we are only measuring associations between county-level poverty and firearm injury health encounters, not causality. In addition, we focused on county-level poverty with the understanding that individual level poverty is heterogenous therefore our findings cannot be ascribed to the individual level. Second, our dataset likely underestimates the burden of firearm injuries due to challenges with coding of injuries and reporting, and this dataset is not a comprehensive report of all statewide firearm injuries. This dataset only includes individuals residing in Maryland who presented to a clinic or hospital in the state, thus we were unable to capture those who did not survive to present to a healthcare setting, those who visited hospitals in neighboring states, those who did not seek care, and perhaps unknown others. These data underestimate the total burden of Maryland firearm injuries in our results, particularly self-harm injuries, a majority of which are known to involve firearms, as many of these individuals do not survive to seek medical care [48,49]. Third, our study involved secondary data analysis using data from several publicly available datasets across institutions. Therefore, categorization of demographic variables such as race and sex, and intent of firearm injury health encounters may vary leading to possible misclassification, especially among gender diverse individuals. Lastly, our study focused on analysis on a small number of counties in Maryland and lack of variability in urbanicity may limit extrapolations beyond our data.

Nonetheless, this study is the first of its kind to provide insight into the association between poverty and firearm injury health encounters across counties in Maryland. It provides important state-specific information that can be useful in guiding firearm injury prevention policy in Maryland. Future studies could focus on other important factors that contribute to firearm injuries such as firearm access and access to mental health services that can further inform policy.

### Conclusion

4.2
In this study of firearm injury health encounters in Maryland from July 2015 to July 2020, we found that counties with the highest poverty concentration had significantly higher rates of firearm injury health encounters overall and across assault, self-harm, and unintentional intents. Our results indicate the importance of addressing poverty in public health interventions and policies aimed at reducing firearm injuries. A multifaceted approach that emphasizes poverty reduction along with other factors involved in firearm injuries, such as legislation on firearm access, is necessary to address the important systemic sociocultural and economic factors that contribute to firearm violence.

## Abstract

### Objective

Firearm injuries are among the four leading causes of injury deaths in the United States. Prior studies have shown the association between poverty and firearm injuries on the national level, but more focused data at the state level has yet to be studied. The objective of this study was to examine the association between county-level poverty and firearm injury health encounters in Maryland, USA.

### Study design

This was an ecological study conducted on counties in Maryland from July 2015–July 2020.

### Methods

This study consisted of residents of all ages with firearm injuries who presented to Maryland healthcare facilities. The outcome variables examined were total firearm injury health encounters and injuries by intent (assault, self-harm, and unintentional). The study exposure was county-level poverty concentration divided into tertiles: 0–7.5%,7.6–12.0%, and 12.1–25.8%. Additional covariates included age, race, sex, and urbanicity.

### Results

Individuals residing in counties in the highest poverty tertile accounted for 16% of the total population but 52% of firearm injury health encounters. Counties in the highest poverty tertile had the highest rates of overall firearm injuries, firearm-related assaults, unintentional, and undetermined injuries, compared to counties in the lowest tertile. However, there was no statistically significant difference in the adjusted firearm self-harm incidence rate comparing counties in the highest poverty tertile to the lowest poverty tertile (IRR: 1.9, 95% CI: 1.0–3.7).

### Conclusion

Higher levels of poverty are associated with increased rates of firearm injury health encounters in Maryland, underscoring the importance of antipoverty initiatives in addressing firearm injuries.

**Keywords:**Poverty, Low-income population, Firearms, Gunshot wound, Gun violence, Maryland

## Introduction

1
Firearm injuries are one of the four leading causes of injury deaths in the United States across all ages, and rates of firearm injuries have risen in the last decade among most age groups, becoming the leading cause of death in individuals under 25 years of age [1,2]. Firearm injuries are an urgent public health concern in the United States, constituting 79% of homicides and 53% of suicides in 2020 [3]. Notably, firearm homicide rates in the United States increased by 35% in 2020 compared to 2019 amidst the COVID-19 pandemic and societal unrest [3]. Increases were also seen at the state level in Maryland with the rate of firearm deaths rising by 36% from 2010 to 2019 compared to a 17% increase nationally [4]. In 2020, the average annual mortality rate from firearm injuries in Maryland was 13.5 deaths per 100,000 people, consistent with the national average mortality rate of 13.7 [5,6]. In Maryland, 62% of firearm injuries are homicides and 36% are suicides, compared to 38% and 60% nationwide [4]. Perhaps more striking is Maryland was ranked among the top 10 states with the highest mean mass shootings, defined as 4 injured or killed in a single incident, per capita from 2015 to 2021 [7].

The devastating effects of firearm injuries extend beyond mortality and result in significant impacts on health and health care utilization. Survivors of firearm injuries have increased rates of hospitalizations, emergency visits, pain diagnoses, substance use disorders, psychiatric disorders, and functional limitations [[[8]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12886088/#bib8), [[9]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12886088/#bib9), [[10]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12886088/#bib10)]. While these health outcomes are common to other traumatic injuries, they have been shown to be worse among survivors of firearm injuries compared to similarly severely injured survivors of motor vehicle accidents [9].

Neighborhood socioeconomic inequalities, like poverty, have also been linked to poorer health outcomes such as obesity, diabetes, cardiovascular disease, and increased overall mortality [11]. Poverty has been associated with numerous adverse health outcomes including that neighborhood poverty and reduced economic opportunity have been associated with firearm injuries and mortality [[[11]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12886088/#bib11), [[12]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12886088/#bib12), [[13]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12886088/#bib13)]. For example, studies conducted on the national level found increased rates of firearm injuries in counties with higher poverty levels [11,12]. This is particularly concerning given the increasing percentage of people experiencing poverty in the United States from 10.5% in 2019 to 11.4% in 2020 [14]. In addition, the gap in income inequality has widened, with income at the top 90th percentile being 13.5 times greater than income for the lowest 10th percentile in 2021, an increase by 4.9% compared to the income gap in 2020 [15]. This increasing exposure to poverty means more people could be affected by its negative health consequences. The burden of firearm injuries in the United States is a multifaceted issue that occurs as a complex interplay of individual, cultural, and socioeconomic risk factors [16]. The role of concentrated poverty on firearm injuries, in particular, is inextricably linked to the persistent effects of systemic and structural racism leading to socioeconomic deprivation, underfunded public services, and lack of opportunity [[[17]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12886088/#bib17), [[18]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12886088/#bib18), [[19]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12886088/#bib19)].

Existing knowledge on the association between poverty and the risk of firearm injuries mainly focuses on their association on the national level. However, this association is not well characterized for individual states. Given the growing burden of firearm injuries, its heterogeneity across states, and the complexity of factors associated with its occurrence, more studies are needed at the state level to provide context specific information to inform targeted public health interventions [3,5,16]. The aim of this study was to examine the association between county-level poverty and firearm injury health encounters in the state of Maryland, USA. We hypothesized that counties with higher poverty concentration would have a higher number of firearm injury health encounters compared to counties with lower poverty concentration.

## Methods

2
### Study design

2.1
We conducted an ecological study of total health encounters for firearm injuries in Maryland from July 1, 2015 to July 31, 2020. Firearm injury health encounters were pooled over the study years and our unit of analysis was the county. This study was acknowledged as exempt by the Institutional Review Board.

### Study exposure

2.2
Our primary exposure of interest was county-level poverty concentration, defined as the percentage of people in the county living below the federal poverty level. Twenty-four counties in Maryland, including Baltimore City, were included in our analysis. County-level poverty was grouped into tertiles (0–7.5%, 7.6–12.0%, and 12.1–25.8%) compared to the standard five categories in previous studies conducted on the national level [11,12], given the distribution of county-level poverty in the smaller number of counties present at the state level. Single-year estimates of county-level poverty concentration from the 2015 U.S. Census Bureau's Small Area Income and Poverty Estimates were used in our analysis as poverty estimates between 2015 and 2020 did not change significantly from year to year; however, it is important to note that these particular data from 2015 through summer 2020 may not reflect the full and substantial economic impacts of the COVID-19 pandemic beginning in 2020 [20].

### Study outcome

2.3
The outcome of this study was the rate of health encounters for overall firearm injuries presenting to healthcare facilities across counties in Maryland measured as injuries per 100,000 person-years. We also measured the rate of firearm injury health encounters by intent given the epidemiologic heterogeneity that exists between different intents. Firearm injury health encounter data from July 2015 to July 2020 was obtained from the State of Maryland's Health Services Cost Review Commission database [21]. This publicly available database collects patient-level demographic and clinic information abstracted from medical records of inpatient and outpatient visits across all acute care hospitals and licensed specialty clinics in Maryland.21 External cause of injury codes from the Tenth Revision of the Internal Statistical Classification of Diseases and Related Health Problems (ICD-10) were used to identify the intent of penetrating trauma by firearms which included assaults (X93-X95), self-harm (X72-X74), unintentional or accidental (W32-W34), and undetermined intent (Y22-Y24). Corresponding ICD-9 codes were also used for the period prior to use of ICD-10 (E9220-E9223, E9550-E9554, E9850-E9854, and E9650-E9654) (See also Table 3). Due to the small number of injuries with undetermined intent and inability to support multivariable analysis, our analysis focused on firearm injury health encounters with determined intent: assault, self-harm, and unintentional. To avoid duplication of individuals in our analysis, we included only initial encounters (denoted by external codes ending in -A) and excluded subsequent and sequelae encounters (denoted by external codes ending in -D and -S, respectively). To prevent including non-Maryland residing individuals, we included only patients with addresses containing Maryland ZIP codes in our analysis.

Annual compressed 5-year population estimates obtained from the US Census Bureau 2020 American Community Survey provided estimates of average population data from 2016 to 2020 by age, race, and sex at the county level [22]. These numbers were used as denominators to calculate injury rates and rate ratios.

### Potential confounders

2.4
Other covariates of interest included age (0–14, 15–24, 25–34, 35–44, and ≥45 years old), sex (male and female), race (White, Black/African-American, and Other [Asian, American Indian/Alaska Native, and Native Hawaiian/Other Pacific Islander]), and urbanicity dichotomized from six categories [urban (large central metropolitan, large fringe metropolitan, medium metropolitan, and small metropolitan) and rural (micropolitan and noncore)]. Age and race were categorized in accordance with published literature on epidemiologic differences in firearm injury rates by age and racial groups [2,11,12]. Urban-rural classification was obtained from the 2013 National Center for Health Statistics, which provided a six-level urban-rural classification for U.S. counties [23]. Urbanicity categories were collapsed based on the National Center for Health Statistics Urban-Rural classification scheme where the most urban categories included metropolitan counties and the most rural categories included nonmetropolitan noncore counties [23].

### Statistical analyses

2.5
Multivariable analyses were conducted using negative binomial regression models. Poisson regression modeling was initially tested but goodness of fit testing revealed a poor fit of our data to the Poisson model due to overdispersion. Thus, negative binomial regression was our final chosen method of modeling. The model included population size divided by 100,000 as an offset term to calculate injury rate per 100,000 population. In addition to this unadjusted model, multivariable models included adjustment for age, sex, race, and urbanicity. For descriptive and multivariable analyses, we calculated total firearm injury health encounter rates and injury rates by intent per 100,000 person-years across age, race, sex, urbanicity, and county-level poverty tertiles. Unadjusted incidence rates were calculated for total firearm injury health encounters and injuries by specific intent across age, race, sex, and urbanicity categories. We also calculated incidence rate ratios (IRR), adjusted for age, race, sex, and urbanicity, for total firearm injury health encounters and injuries by specific intent across county-level poverty concentration to compare rates between poverty tertiles.

## Results

3
### Firearm injury health encounters in the Maryland population

3.1
According to 2016–2020 Census data, an average of 5,481,115 people resided in Maryland per year. Overall, individuals tended to be older adults (with 44.5% being ≥45 years old), female (51.8%), and White (59.8%) (Table 1). 97.4% of individuals resided in urban counties. A total of 1404 firearm injury health encounters were observed in this dataset comprised of reporting from acute care and subspecialty Maryland hospitals from July 2015 to July 2020 for individuals residing in Maryland. Among the encounters captured in the dataset, 63% were assaults, 5.1% were self-harm, 29.1% were unintentional, and 2.8% were of undetermined intent. Individuals residing in counties in the highest poverty tertile comprised 16% of the total population and 52% of firearm injury health encounters. Those living in counties in the lowest poverty tertile had the lowest proportion of firearm injury health encounters at 16.7%. The majority of firearm injury health encounters in each poverty tertile were assaults with the proportion of assault injuries increasing with higher poverty tertiles (47.6%, 59.5%, and 70.2%, respectively). While the proportion of firearm assaults increased with each poverty category, the proportion of self-harm, unintentional, or undetermined firearm injury health encounters decreased with each poverty tertile. ### Firearm injury health encounters and county-level poverty

3.3
Adjusting for age, race, sex, and urbanicity, individuals living in counties in the highest poverty tertile had 3.6 times higher (95% CI: 2.7–4.8) total firearm injury health encounters compared to those living in counties in the lowest poverty tertile and this difference was statistically significant (Fig. 1). Those living in counties in the intermediate poverty tertile had an adjusted 1.2 times higher (95% CI: 0.9–1.6) total firearm injury health encounters compared to those living in the lowest county poverty tertile, but this difference was not statistically significant.

We observed statistically significant increases in the adjusted firearm injury health encounters incidence rate ratios in counties in the highest poverty tertile category for firearm-related assaults (IRR: 5.5, 95% CI: 3.8–8.0), and unintentional (IRR: 3.2, 95% CI: 2.1–4.6),However, there was no statistically significant difference in the adjusted firearm self-harm incidence rate when comparing individuals residing in counties in the highest poverty tertile (IRR: 1.9, 95% CI: 1.0–3.7) to those residing in the lowest poverty tertile.

## Discussion

4
In this ecological study, counties in the highest poverty tertile had higher rates of overall firearm injury health encounters including assault, self-harm, and unintentional intent compared to counties in the lowest poverty tertile. This association was present, for most injury intents, after adjusting for other relevant factors such as age, race, sex, and urbanicity, that are known to contribute to the occurrence of firearm injuries [11,12,24]. This study is consistent with similar studies conducted on the national level demonstrating higher rates of firearm injuries in counties with higher poverty concentration. To our knowledge, this is the first study evaluating county poverty concentration and firearm injury health encounters across various intents in the State of Maryland.

The United States has one of the highest poverty rates among developed countries with the greatest burden among racial minority communities [17]. Poverty is a multifaceted construct that goes beyond income and includes economic well-being, social exclusion, lack of basic education and employment opportunities, and inadequate housing [17,25]. It is recognized as one of the most significant factors contributing to poor health outcomes [26]. Prior studies have linked poverty to violence and subsequent injuries, mental health conditions, and communicable and non-communicable diseases [11,12,17]. This impact of poverty is consistent with our study findings that show that individuals residing in counties with the highest poverty concentration comprise 52% of firearm injury health encounters in the state though they make up only 16% of the total population.

The link between poverty and firearm violence intersects with other deeply entrenched socioeconomic factors like racism [17]. Persistent systemic and structural racism in the United States contribute to the higher burden of firearm violence in racial minority communities [18]. In this study, we observed higher rates of overall health encounter firearm injuries and firearm-related assault and unintentional injuries in Black individuals compared to their White counterparts. Systemic racism plays a role in these findings through concentrated poverty, socioeconomic deprivation, and increased surveillance and harassment by law enforcement in minority communities [18]. While we did not identify which firearm injury health encounters occurred due to police encounters in our analysis; there is strong evidence linking policing and firearm violence among racial minorities [18,27,28]. In contrast to the pattern of increased firearm-related assaults among Black individuals, we found higher rates of firearm-related self-harm in White individuals, which is consistent with prior literature [12,29]. American Indian/Alaska Native populations are second to White populations in rates of firearm-related suicides nationally [12,29], but the population characteristics in the State of Maryland did now allow for this analysis.

We observed significantly higher firearm injury health encounter rates in counties in the highest poverty tertile compared to those in the lowest poverty tertile, but we did not observe significant increases when comparing counties in the intermediate poverty tertile to those in the lowest poverty tertile. This suggests the impact of poverty may be more pronounced at higher poverty levels. The significantly higher firearm injury health encounter rates seen in counties in the highest poverty tertile was consistent across overall firearm injuries and intents, except for firearm-related self-harm injuries which did not show significant differences in firearm injury rates across poverty tertiles. This suggests that there are other factors that contribute to the association between county-level poverty and firearm-related self-harm such as firearm prevalence and access to mental health services [12,30] that were not accounted for in this study due to limited data.

The highest rates of overall health encounter firearm injuries and firearm-related assaults and unintentional injuries were observed among those aged 15–24. This is consistent with data from the literature demonstrating sharp increases in firearm-related injuries in US youth, particularly in the 15-24 year-old age group, with homicides increasing by 14% over the past decade [2]. Increased access to firearms has been cited as one of the main causes of this phenomenon [2]. Federal law restricts licensed dealers from selling or transferring handguns and long guns to minors, and Maryland law generally prohibits anyone under age 21 from possessing a handgun or other regulated firearm as well as prohibiting any person from selling or transferring a firearm or ammunition to a person under age 18 [2,[[31]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12886088/#bib31), [[32]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12886088/#bib32), [[33]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12886088/#bib33), [[34]](https://pmc.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/articles/PMC12886088/#bib34)]. In addition, the presence of firearms in the home is a significant risk factor in firearm-related injuries among youth [35] with estimates of firearm ownership in Maryland between 16 and 20% [36,37]. While studies show firearm-related self-harm has also been increasing among the 15–24 age group [38,39], we observed the highest rates of firearm-related self-harm among the 35–44 age group followed by similar rates in the 15–24 age group and ≥45 age group. This effect may be due to known increases in firearm self-harm rates with age [40] and firearms being the most common method of self-harm in older adults [41].

Differences in firearm injury rates are known to exist between rural and urban counties [11,12,42]. In this study, we observed higher overall firearm injury health encounter rates and firearm-related assaults in urban counties compared to rural counties. In contrast, we found higher rates of unintentional and self-harm firearm injury health encounters in rural counties compared to urban counties, consistent with previous studies [12,42]. This finding highlights the probability of other mechanisms that influence the association between urbanicity and firearm injuries by self-harm and unintentional intent compared to other intents. This includes higher lethality of means of suicide and increased accessibility to firearms in rural counties [12,24]. In Maryland specifically, victims of firearm suicide in rural counties were more likely to use long guns compared to most urban counties even after adjusting for demographic factors and hunting season [24]. While data on firearm ownership by county in Maryland is limited, one of the top reasons for gun ownership in the United States is hunting, and rural areas are known to engage more in hunting activities [43].

Our study findings indicate that county-level poverty is associated with the occurrence of firearm injury health encounters in Maryland. We emphasize that reducing firearm injuries in Maryland, a state with a higher firearm homicide rate compared to the national rate, requires a multisector approach including legislation on restricting firearm access, addressing attitudes towards gun violence, and tackling social determinants of health like poverty from the individual to the societal level. The association between poverty and firearm injuries intersects with other socioeconomic factors beyond income status including inadequate housing and a limited number of and access to resources [17,25]. These factors contribute to a breakdown in social cohesion described as a lack of mutual trust among community members that contributes to firearm violence [44]. Sustainable reduction of firearm injuries therefore requires consideration of these factors in the creation and implementation of policies. The Baltimore Safe Streets Intervention is an example of an existing community-based program that has shown significant results in improving youth attitudes towards gun violence, a known factor contributing to gun violence in high-risk youth [45]. Community efforts such as these that address sociocultural factors that underlie poverty, policies that target job, food, and housing insecurities, and higher-level societal interventions on restricting gun access and promoting safe gun storage are necessary to address the complexity of the factors contributing to firearm violence [46,47].

### Study limitations and strengths

4.1
This study has several limitations. First, because this is an ecological study, we are only measuring associations between county-level poverty and firearm injury health encounters, not causality. In addition, we focused on county-level poverty with the understanding that individual level poverty is heterogenous therefore our findings cannot be ascribed to the individual level. Second, our dataset likely underestimates the burden of firearm injuries due to challenges with coding of injuries and reporting, and this dataset is not a comprehensive report of all statewide firearm injuries. This dataset only includes individuals residing in Maryland who presented to a clinic or hospital in the state, thus we were unable to capture those who did not survive to present to a healthcare setting, those who visited hospitals in neighboring states, those who did not seek care, and perhaps unknown others. These data underestimate the total burden of Maryland firearm injuries in our results, particularly self-harm injuries, a majority of which are known to involve firearms, as many of these individuals do not survive to seek medical care [48,49]. Third, our study involved secondary data analysis using data from several publicly available datasets across institutions. Therefore, categorization of demographic variables such as race and sex, and intent of firearm injury health encounters may vary leading to possible misclassification, especially among gender diverse individuals. Lastly, our study focused on analysis on a small number of counties in Maryland and lack of variability in urbanicity may limit extrapolations beyond our data.

Nonetheless, this study is the first of its kind to provide insight into the association between poverty and firearm injury health encounters across counties in Maryland. It provides important state-specific information that can be useful in guiding firearm injury prevention policy in Maryland. Future studies could focus on other important factors that contribute to firearm injuries such as firearm access and access to mental health services that can further inform policy.

### Conclusion

4.2
In this study of firearm injury health encounters in Maryland from July 2015 to July 2020, we found that counties with the highest poverty concentration had significantly higher rates of firearm injury health encounters overall and across assault, self-harm, and unintentional intents. Our results indicate the importance of addressing poverty in public health interventions and policies aimed at reducing firearm injuries. A multifaceted approach that emphasizes poverty reduction along with other factors involved in firearm injuries, such as legislation on firearm access, is necessary to address the important systemic sociocultural and economic factors that contribute to firearm violence.

Why This Topic Is Important

 The death of any young person is a tragedy. High death rates also can be an indicator of larger system issues, such as community violence or barriers to health care. In the U.S., unintentional injuries are the leading cause of death among young people ages 1-24: For children ages 1-4, the most common mechanism is drowning; for 5- to 19-year-olds, it is motor vehicle crashes; for young adults ages 20-24, it is poisonings, nearly all from drug overdose (1, 2). Other leading causes of death among children and young adults include suicide, homicide, cancer, heart disease, and birth defects (1). In 2020, firearms overtook motor vehicles as the leading mechanism of injury death among U.S. children ages 0-17 (2).  
  
 Death rates from injuries, and overall death rates, generally are higher for boys than girls (2). Disparities by race/ethnicity also persist, statewide and nationally; e.g., among groups with data, African American/black and American Indian/Alaska Native children and youth have had the highest death rates for many years (3). Many fatal injuries can be prevented through environmental, behavioral, social, and legislative change (4).

How Children Are Faring

 In 2015-2017, the death rate among California young people ages 1-24 was 29.8 per 100,000, lower than the U.S. rate of 40.9 deaths per 100,000. After declining between 2004-2006 and 2013-2015, statewide rates have risen in recent years, echoing national trends. Across counties with data, child and young adult death rates vary widely, from 18.4 per 100,000 (Yolo) to 76 per 100,000 (Calaveras) in 2015-2017.  
  
 Young adults ages 20-24 consistently have higher death rates (64.9 per 100,000 in 2015-2017) than other age groups in California, while children ages 5-14 have the lowest (10 per 100,000 in 2015-2017). Since 2000-2002, African American/black and American Indian/Alaska Native youth have experienced the highest rates of death among racial/ethnic groups with data statewide. Both in California and the nation as a whole, unintentional injuries—such as drownings, car crashes, and poisonings (including overdoses)—are the leading cause of death for children and young adults overall, for all age groups, and for all racial/ethnic groups with data except African American/black youth, for whom homicide is the leading cause of death.  
  
 In 2020, California young people ages 0-24 died of firearm injuries at a rate of 5.6 per 100,000, an increase of around 30% compared with 2019. Of the 692 firearm-related deaths among children and young adults statewide in 2020, boys and young men accounted for the vast majority (616). Homicide and suicide are the most common causes of firearm-related death across gender and age groups. Disparities exist in firearm death rates by race/ethnicity, statewide and nationally. In California, the firearm death rate among African American/black youth in 2020 (24.8 per 100,000 in 2020) was four times higher than the rate for Hispanic/Latino youth (5.8 per 100,000), seven times higher than that for white youth (3.4 per 100,000), and 16 times that for Asian youth (1.5 per 100,000). 

Policy Implications

 Most child and young adult deaths are due to preventable causes (1). Public policies aimed at prevention, education, and support of young people and their families can address these causes.  
  
 Policy options that could reduce child and young adult deaths include: 
*   Strengthening, enforcing, and promoting awareness of motor vehicle safety laws concerning car seats, seat belts, distracted and drunk driving, and graduated driver licensing systems (2)
*   Promoting safe, stable, and caring relationships between caregivers and children and addressing risk factors associated with child maltreatment such as neighborhood economic stress and family poverty (3)
*   Addressing depression and preventing youth suicide by providing routine and accessible mental health screening and services; also going beyond the prevention and treatment of problems to promoting positive mental health (4)
*   Reducing student violence, substance use, and other high-risk behaviors by promoting policies that foster positive school climates where students feel safe, connected, and supported (5, 6)
*   Addressing risk factors for gang involvement and violent behavior by strengthening youth connections to family and school, improving community supervision and engagement, and helping young people develop social-emotional skills (7)
*   Continuing efforts to ensure that all infants, children, and young adults—particularly those with special health care needs—and their families have access to quality medical care that is affordable, timely, comprehensive, continuous, patient centered, and culturally appropriate (8)
*   Supporting continued pediatric cancer research to promote advances in the understanding of risk factors and treatments (9)

Why This Topic Is Important

 The death of any young person is a tragedy. High death rates also can be an indicator of larger system issues, such as community violence or barriers to health care. In the U.S., unintentional injuries are the leading cause of death among young people ages 1-24: For children ages 1-4, the most common mechanism is drowning; for 5- to 19-year-olds, it is motor vehicle crashes; for young adults ages 20-24, it is poisonings, nearly all from drug overdose (1, 2). Other leading causes of death among children and young adults include suicide, homicide, cancer, heart disease, and birth defects (1). In 2020, firearms overtook motor vehicles as the leading mechanism of injury death among U.S. children ages 0-17 (2).  
  
 Death rates from injuries, and overall death rates, generally are higher for boys than girls (2). Disparities by race/ethnicity also persist, statewide and nationally; e.g., among groups with data, African American/black and American Indian/Alaska Native children and youth have had the highest death rates for many years (3). Many fatal injuries can be prevented through environmental, behavioral, social, and legislative change (4).

How Children Are Faring

 In 2015-2017, the death rate among California young people ages 1-24 was 29.8 per 100,000, lower than the U.S. rate of 40.9 deaths per 100,000. After declining between 2004-2006 and 2013-2015, statewide rates have risen in recent years, echoing national trends. Across counties with data, child and young adult death rates vary widely, from 18.4 per 100,000 (Yolo) to 76 per 100,000 (Calaveras) in 2015-2017.  
  
 Young adults ages 20-24 consistently have higher death rates (64.9 per 100,000 in 2015-2017) than other age groups in California, while children ages 5-14 have the lowest (10 per 100,000 in 2015-2017). Since 2000-2002, African American/black and American Indian/Alaska Native youth have experienced the highest rates of death among racial/ethnic groups with data statewide. Both in California and the nation as a whole, unintentional injuries—such as drownings, car crashes, and poisonings (including overdoses)—are the leading cause of death for children and young adults overall, for all age groups, and for all racial/ethnic groups with data except African American/black youth, for whom homicide is the leading cause of death.  
  
 In 2020, California young people ages 0-24 died of firearm injuries at a rate of 5.6 per 100,000, an increase of around 30% compared with 2019. Of the 692 firearm-related deaths among children and young adults statewide in 2020, boys and young men accounted for the vast majority (616). Homicide and suicide are the most common causes of firearm-related death across gender and age groups. Disparities exist in firearm death rates by race/ethnicity, statewide and nationally. In California, the firearm death rate among African American/black youth in 2020 (24.8 per 100,000 in 2020) was four times higher than the rate for Hispanic/Latino youth (5.8 per 100,000), seven times higher than that for white youth (3.4 per 100,000), and 16 times that for Asian youth (1.5 per 100,000). 

Policy Implications

 Most child and young adult deaths are due to preventable causes (1). Public policies aimed at prevention, education, and support of young people and their families can address these causes.  
  
 Policy options that could reduce child and young adult deaths include: 
*   Strengthening, enforcing, and promoting awareness of motor vehicle safety laws concerning car seats, seat belts, distracted and drunk driving, and graduated driver licensing systems (2)
*   Promoting safe, stable, and caring relationships between caregivers and children and addressing risk factors associated with child maltreatment such as neighborhood economic stress and family poverty (3)
*   Addressing depression and preventing youth suicide by providing routine and accessible mental health screening and services; also going beyond the prevention and treatment of problems to promoting positive mental health (4)
*   Reducing student violence, substance use, and other high-risk behaviors by promoting policies that foster positive school climates where students feel safe, connected, and supported (5, 6)
*   Addressing risk factors for gang involvement and violent behavior by strengthening youth connections to family and school, improving community supervision and engagement, and helping young people develop social-emotional skills (7)
*   Continuing efforts to ensure that all infants, children, and young adults—particularly those with special health care needs—and their families have access to quality medical care that is affordable, timely, comprehensive, continuous, patient centered, and culturally appropriate (8)
*   Supporting continued pediatric cancer research to promote advances in the understanding of risk factors and treatments (9)

## Abstract

Using data from the Centers for Disease Control and Prevention’s Web-based Injury Statistics Query and Reporting System, we analyzed trends in firearm suicide across the life course, comparing age-related trends over time (2015–20 versus 1999–2014) and stratified by differences in state firearm policy environments. Overall, we found stable trends in firearm suicide rates across the life course, although with higher overall rates across all age groups in 2015–20 versus in 1999–2014. Ages 14–16 was the only age group with an accelerating life-course trend in firearm suicide rates in 2015–20 versus in 1999–2014. The state policy environment was associated with significant differences in firearm suicide, with an average of 4.62 more deaths per 100,000 people per year in states with less- versus more-strict environments. This was in contrast to nonfirearm suicides, for which we observed no consistent differences between states. The largest overall differences in firearm suicide between states occurred in adulthood through middle age. These findings can inform further research on health care–based approaches to reducing firearm suicide, such as health care screening for firearm ownership, screening for suicide risk among firearm owners, and motivational interviewing to promote safe firearm storage.

## Study Data And Methods

### DATA

We examined how firearm suicide varied across the life course over time and across state policy environments, using aggregate January 1999–December 2020 data from WISQARS. We first compared average (mean) crude rates of firearm suicide for each age-year in the period between 2015 and 2020, which was a period of increased firearm deaths, with means observed in the period between 1999 and 2014, a period of relative stability in firearm deaths. Crude rates were defined as the number of firearm suicides per 100,000 people per year.

We further explored age-related trends in firearm suicide by calculating first-difference changes in firearm suicide rates. First differences were calculated by subtracting crude firearm mortality rates at a given age (y age) from crude rates among those one year older (y age+1). We performed this analysis for 1999–2014 and 2015–20. First-difference rates were plotted as time-series line plots, with age-year along the _x_ axis and firearm suicide rates along the _y_ axis.

### ANALYSIS

Using a longitudinal panel design, we then compared firearm suicide rates for each age-year between states with less- versus more-strict firearm policy environments. To categorize states’ firearm policy environments, we used 2021 Annual Gun Law Scorecard grades19 (see online appendix exhibits A1 and A2).20 Such scales, ranking states on overall “permissiveness” of firearm legislation, effectively characterize state firearm policy environments while avoiding statistical complications that can arise from tabulating laws and policies individually.21 States that received a C grade or lower were classified as having less-strict environments, whereas those that received a C+ or higher were classified as having more-strict environments. We then examined firearm suicide rates by age-year, using kernel-weighted local polynomial smoothing (univariate nonparametric regression) to examine differences in trend by firearm policy category (less versus more strict).

We then compared firearm suicide rates with nonfirearm and total suicide rates between states with less- versus more-strict firearm environments during 2015–20. First, we used kernel-weighted local polynomial smoothing and univariate nonparametric regression to visualize state differences. Second, we calculated average differences between states in annual suicide rates (total, firearm, and nonfirearm) across the total population (all ages) and by life-course decades (ages 12–20 through 71–80). We used generalized linear models (Gaussian family, identity link, exchangeable correlation matrix) for all analyses. In analyses of life-course decades, we used each state as the panel identifier and generalized estimating equations to fit population-averaged models. Suicide rates were modeled as a function of Giffords score category19 (less versus more strict) for the total population (all ages) and each life-course decade. We then calculated the difference in trend for each decade by modeling mortality rate as a function of the interaction between Giffords score category and age-year.

The CDC WISQARS interface suppresses fatal injury data in cells with fewer than ten deaths, which led to suppressed data for lower and higher age-years and for smaller states (for example, firearm suicides for age-year eighty in Rhode Island). We therefore restricted the age range to 12–80 in analyses of life-course decades and excluded Hawaii, Rhode Island, and Washington, D.C., which had substantial missing data. In the final sample, missing data were satisfactory in analyses of total suicide (3.0 percent) and firearm suicide (8.6 percent) but were somewhat higher for nonfirearm suicide (15.2 percent). Acknowledging that missing values were between zero and nine deaths, we conducted sensitivity analyses using univariate truncated regression imputation to estimate deaths between zero and nine (twenty imputations), based on state and age trends. In additional sensitivity analyses, we substituted five deaths for deaths between zero and nine.

As additional sensitivity analyses, we included probability weights to account for state population during the study period, an alternative Annual Gun Law Scorecard grade grouping (categorizing states that received grades of A to C− as more strict and D+ to F as less strict), and another analysis using 2015 Annual Gun Law Scorecard grades to test for possible differences in grades over time.

### LIMITATIONS

Our study had several limitations. Although we demonstrated strong associations between state firearm policies and suicide, our data did not permit specific causal inferences regarding the impact of firearm regulations. Cultural, demographic, and economic differences between states, as well as baseline differences in firearm accessibility, household firearm ownership, and health system access, are likely correlated with state firearm policy environments and may also influence firearm suicide rates. Second, we extracted death counts by age-year, which resulted in suppression of death counts for certain ages with fewer than ten deaths, especially for extreme ages and small states. We were thus forced to exclude Hawaii, Rhode Island, and Washington, D.C., which had substantial missing data. These places had stricter firearm policies, and their exclusion because of low death counts would have biased study findings toward the null.

## Study Results

Firearm suicide rates increased rapidly with age during the second decade of life (exhibit 1) in each of the time periods we examined. Rates exhibited a limited, albeit steady, increase into middle age (through age sixty), and then a second period of more rapid increase in ages older than sixty. Firearm suicides rates increased in 2015–20 relative to 1999–2014, but age-year trends followed a similar trajectory across the life course, with one notable exception: an earlier peak of acceleration among adolescents age fourteen in 2015–20, instead of peaking at age sixteen as during the previous period (appendix exhibit A3).20

When we stratified our analysis by Annual Gun Law Scorecard grades, we found that less-strict states exhibited steeper increases in firearm suicide mortality during adolescence and had persistently higher rates over the life course (exhibit 2). In analyses comparing firearm suicides, nonfirearm suicides, and total suicides across state policy environments, we observed higher rates of firearm suicide and total suicide in states with less-strict policy environments (exhibits 2, 3, and 4 and appendix exhibit A4) than in those with more-strict policy environments.20 Overall firearm suicide rates were higher by 4.62 deaths per 100,000 residents per year (95% confidence interval: 2.82, 6.41) in states with less- compared with more-strict policy environments (appendix exhibit A5).20 This was in contrast to nonfirearm suicide rates, for which we observed no significant difference between states (−0.19 deaths per 100,000 per year; 95% CI: −1.17, 0.78).

Across the life course, the largest increase in differences between less- versus more-strict states occurred during the transition from adolescence to young adulthood (exhibit 4). Among people in their teens (ages 12–20), annual firearm suicide rates were 4.36 deaths per 100,000 (95% CI: 2.11, 6.61) higher in states with less-versus more-strict policy environments compared with 6.62 deaths per 100,000 (95% CI:4.11, 9.12) higher among people in their twenties (ages 21–30). Correspondingly, in analyses of acceleration (that is, change in firearm suicide rates by age-year), we observed a larger rate of acceleration among those in their teens by 0.55 additional deaths per 100,000 people per year (95% CI: 0.23–0.86) in states with less- versus more-strict firearm policies. In all remaining decades, firearm suicide rates remained elevated, with the largest total difference between states in adulthood through middle age.

Results remained substantively unchanged in sensitivity analyses, using univariate imputation and substitution to account for suppressed death counts (appendix exhibits A6–A9).20 Sensitivity analyses using state population weights also revealed similar findings (appendix exhibit A10), as did those using alternative grade groupings (appendix exhibit A11) and 2015 grades (appendix exhibit A12).20

## Discussion

Our study examined rates and trends in US firearm suicide across the life course. Our findings corroborated prior research showing that firearm suicides rise with age in early adulthood, with a second period of acceleration later in life. We add to this literature by comparing a period of higher overall firearm mortality (2015–20) with a preceding period that was relatively stable (1999–2014). Despite higher overall rates of suicide deaths between 2015 and 2020, trends across the life course were strikingly similar to those in previous years, with the notable exception of accelerating suicide rates earlier in adolescence. We also found significantly higher firearm suicide rates in states with less-strict firearm policy environments. Overall, we estimated that states with less-strict firearm policies experienced, on average, 4.62 more firearm suicides per 100,000 residents per year than states with more-strict firearm policies.

Our findings have several implications. First, age-related trends appear to have been stable during the past two decades. This observation suggests that age-specific factors, such as underdevelopment of neurocognitive risk aversion in adolescents22,23 or experiences of concomitant financial and medical hardships in older adults,24 may predictably augment the risk for firearm-related suicide at particular life stages. Front-line clinicians, researchers, health system leaders, and policy makers should acknowledge differences in risk across the life course, tailoring research and interventions to unique periods of risk acceleration that occur consistently in adolescence and older age. For example, the American Academy of Pediatrics’ Bright Futures initiative currently recommends screening all pediatric patients at least annually for in-home firearm exposure,25 but there are no specific recommendations to screen adults for firearm possession and safety, even though total suicide risk is highest among adults, particularly in states with less-strict firearm policy environments. This is despite evidence of the acceptability and effectiveness of health care–based interventions.12–14 For example, training clinicians to perform motivational interviews related to firearm safety has been shown to enhance safe firearm handling and storage.14 Other studies have found that programs providing safety devices that prevent firearm operation when activated can be particularly effective.12

Second, the finding of stable age-related trends had one notable exception in recent years: a younger age of acceleration in adolescent suicide. Interestingly, adolescent suicide rates experienced a surge in the 1980s, which some scholars attributed to sociocultural shifts (for example, increased divorce rates) and increased firearm availability.26 Our novel findings raise concerns about another period of environmental or sociocultural shifts putting younger children at even higher risk for suicide.

Recent studies document related findings, showing significant increases in teenage suicidal ideation and hopelessness,27 emergency department visits for mental health and behavioral emergencies,28 and completed suicide,29,30 all of which have been shown to be exacerbated during the COVID-19 pandemic.31,32 In response to such trends, US Surgeon General Vivek Murthy has called for increased mental health treatment and support for young people, citing social media use, adverse childhood experiences, and economic instability as key risks in today’s sociocultural environment.33 Our findings underscore the importance of risk screening, care coordination, and mental health support for adolescents, given evidence that ages 14–16 is the only age group that exhibited accelerating life-course suicide risk. Indeed, our findings do not merely indicate increased rates of adolescent suicide during a unique period but also show a fundamental shift in age-related trends during adolescence.

Finally, we observed two notable findings in states with stricter firearm policies. Although we could not directly address causality, stricter state-level policies appeared to have been associated with modest but significantly lower accelerations in adolescent firearm suicide (ages 12–20), and lower rates persisted across the life course. Stricter firearm policy environments were associated with 4.62 fewer deaths per 100,000 annually than was the case in less-strict policy environments. To put this number into context, overall US firearm homicide rates varied from 4.05 to 5.85 per 100,000 per year during the same period.34 In other words, the difference in firearm suicide rates between states with less-versus more-strict policy environments was nearly as large as the nation’s overall firearm homicide rate during the same period. Moreover, differences in state firearm policies were not associated with significant differences in nonfirearm suicide. States with less-strict firearm regulations thus displayed markedly higher overall suicide rates.

These findings build on existing scholarship, linking firearm suicide to more firearm ownership and less firearm regulation.5,6 Firearms are the most lethal and common method of suicide completion and are particularly dangerous in combination with impulsive behavior.34 Widespread firearm availability with no recommendations for screening, especially among people experiencing mental health crises, is thus a critical and often-missed opportunity for prevention in clinical care.

## Conclusion

Our analyses underscore several findings. We reiterate the urgency of addressing the recent acceleration in firearm suicide among younger teens,33 but we also note the relative stability of firearm suicide across the remaining life course. We urge clinicians and researchers to consider this consistency of firearm suicide trends across the life course, especially as they persist through middle and older age, in investigating the acceptability, feasibility, and effectiveness of health care–based screening and interventions to reduce suicide mortality.

Finally, we found that firearm policy environments were associated with large total differences in firearm suicides—a gap that is roughly equivalent to the US firearm homicide rate—with the largest differences among young and middle-aged adults (ages 21–60). Although middle-aged residents of states with less-strict firearm policies make an unlikely portrait of firearm-violence victims in the US, our data suggest that this group warrants particularly close attention to better address the continuing threat of firearm violence and suicide.
